column3: What it actually means in the spec

“No explicit anchor was set”. The default for a **text‑only** symbol is `center`. Most place‑name layers never set `text-anchor` because they rely on the default, so they satisfy this part of the test.
“Treat the symbol as a point feature”. This is the default for **any** symbol layer that is not a line‑placement (e.g., road‑labels, POI icons, shields, etc.). Again, it’s a very generic flag.

column1: Together they describe *almost every* point‑based symbol layer that does **not** override the default text‑anchor – which is the majority of place‑name layers. Hence the false‑positives.

Real shield layers often **do** set `text-anchor` (e.g., `center` or `bottom`) and they may also use `symbol-placement: line` for “road‑shield‑along‑the‑road” styles. So the heuristic also **misses** many genuine shields.

The route number is usually inserted via a token (`{ref}`, `{network}`, `{route}` etc.). If the field contains a token, you know the layer is meant to display a dynamic route identifier.
Place‑name layers also use tokens (`{name}`, `{name_en}`), but you can differentiate by the *token name*: `ref`, `ref_number`, `route`, `network`, `shield`, etc.
Shields are usually allowed to overlap other symbols because they sit on top of the road line.
Shields often use a very specific font (e.g., `""Open Sans Bold""` or a custom “shield” font) and a relatively large size (12‑16 px).
Shields are often scaled (`icon-size` > 1) to match road‑width.
Shields may be optional at low zooms – these flags are common on shield layers.
Many shield layers filter on a property like `""ref""` or `""network""` to ensure they only draw where a route reference exists.
